title: Boards Café
subtitle: Café operations backend
role: Backend development (provided in my project brief); individual module authorship is not established by source review.
desc: A structured café operations API connecting menu categories, product variants, pricing, and sales orders.
problem: Café teams need consistent menu information and reliable order totals without scattering business rules across interfaces.
users: Café staff, administrators, and frontend developers integrating the operations API.
solution: A modular Django backend with model constraints, serializer validation, authenticated order operations, and generated API documentation.
architecture: Django apps separate menu, sales, users, roles, and inventory. Categories contain products; products have variants. Orders contain line items that retain a snapshot of product names and prices.
features: Category, product, and variant models with uniqueness constraints.
Validation prevents negative effective variant prices and invalid product/variant combinations.
Order serializers calculate line totals, subtotals, and fixed or percentage discounts using Decimal arithmetic.
Order queries are scoped to their creator unless the requester is staff. Updates and deletion are limited to draft orders.
Routes include /api/menu/categories/, /api/menu/products/, /api/menu/variants/, /api/v1/sales/orders/, and /api/v1/docs/.
planned: Runtime verification of menu and sales flows against the deployed environment.
Independent test execution and deployment validation.
decision: Snapshotting product and variant names with unit prices preserves the meaning of historical order lines when menu information changes. Atomic writes keep order creation and its items in one transaction.
outcome: The inspected source contains menu and sales models, validation, and API routes. Authentication test files exist, but were not executed during this portfolio review. Payment processing is outside the scope of this case study.
reflection: Engineering takeaway: preserve historical business records and enforce pricing rules on the server. A personal retrospective is still to be added.
missing: Module-level contribution and team ownership details.
Passing test reports and production readiness evidence.
Deployment health could not be confirmed during review.

title: REACH

desc: A lending prototype exploring how business information can support financing assessment for businesses with limited traditional collateral.
problem: Businesses may struggle to demonstrate creditworthiness when financing depends heavily on traditional collateral.
solution: Explore a structured application journey that combines business identification, tax information, loan purpose, and an explainable assessment.
architecture: The repository contains applicant, approver, and admin views. A TypeScript eligibility module looks up mock RDB, RRA, and credit-reference records; these are simulated datasets, not live institutional integrations.
features: Applicant application, eligibility, loan-purpose, identity, and tracking pages are present.
A TypeScript function calculates illustrative eligibility, reasons, conditions, and repayment estimates from mock records.
The inspected auth context uses a default demo profile; it does not establish production authentication.
planned: Authorized RRA and RDB integrations and an appropriate credit-reference data connection.
Server-side validation, persistent applications, and a verified authentication backend.
Review of assessment rules before any use in real lending.
decision: Keeping lookup and eligibility calculations in a separate module makes the prototype logic easier to inspect. The demo must keep simulated assessment distinct from actual lending decisions.
outcome: Source confirms a frontend prototype and mock-data assessment logic. No live institutional connection or real financing outcome has been verified.
reflection: Engineering takeaway: explain the data behind a decision and keep prototype assumptions visible. Personal lessons and user feedback are still to be documented.

title: Blood Supply Flow Monitoring

role: Information systems project work, as described in my brief. Detailed authorship and implementation responsibilities remain to be recorded.
desc: An academic system exploring blood-stock visibility, hospital requests, transfers, expiration, and coordination with the Rwanda Biomedical Centre.
problem: Hospitals and RBC need better visibility into supply, demand, expiry, and transfers to coordinate blood availability.
users: Hospital stock managers, RBC coordinators, and system administrators.
solution: Model supply and demand as traceable records and expose inventory calculations and request workflows through an API prototype.
architecture: The inspected repository contains a React frontend and a FastAPI backend. SQLAlchemy models describe BloodUnit, TransfusionRequest, and Transfer. Next.js and PostgreSQL remain the intended direction from my brief, rather than a verified completed migration.
features: Backend source exposes blood-unit registration and listing, request creation and listing, and transfer creation routes.
Inventory logic implements stock balance, expiry calculation, and simple forecasting helpers.

planned: Validate hospital requests → allocation → transfer → stock update as a complete workflow.

decision: Separating inventory balance calculations from API handlers makes the arithmetic inspectable. Stock balance alone does not establish complete clinical traceability or safe deployment.
outcome: Source confirms a prototype API and inventory model, not an operational hospital or RBC production deployment.
reflection: Engineering takeaway: connect each inventory change to a documented event. Personal research findings and stakeholder feedback still need to be added.
